newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus raps Russian liberals in journalist row.
newsitem.headline: Belarus raps Russian liberals in journalist row.

text.p: Belarus, which wants to forge a close union with Russia, on Thursday defended its decision to withdraw accreditation from a Russian journalist and angrily accused Moscow liberals of meddling in its affairs.

"An (anti-Belarus) campaign is being unleashed by the lads who lead a Western way of life, receive Western salaries and hate the right of small states to an independent policy," Foreign Minister Ivan Antonovich told Reuters.

He named no names but was clearly responding to comments by Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, a pro-market reformer, that Moscow would defend the rights of its journalists "wherever they work, be it Belarus, North Korea or Cuba".

Nemtsov on Wednesday slammed Belarus' decision to annul the accreditation of Pavel Sheremet, the Minsk bureau chief of the Russian Public Television (ORT) company. Belarus accuses him of insulting and tendentious reporting, charges he denies.
"First we will get explanations...then conclusions will be drawn. Russia has quite a variety of methods to protect its journalists," Nemtsov said.
Antonovich fired back on Thursday: "If Russia presses the levers of pressure we will do the same. We have enough of them."
But he added that Belarus would not be provoked into actions that might harm the interests of the two states' integration.
The Foreign Ministry also issued a statement on Thursday protesting about what it described as "an information war" waged by certain elements of the Russian mass media against Belarus.

"Instead of an adequate reaction and efforts to understand (the situation) an escalation of accusations is continuing which...fuels tensions and meddles in the internal affairs of a sovereign republic," it said.

Nemtsov, seen as critical of Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko's authoritarian policies, said Minsk's action against Sheremet contradicted a Russian-Belarus accord signed earlier this year on closer integration.

The document was watered down under pressure from Moscow liberals such as Nemtsov to prevent Lukashenko playing a role in Russia's policy. A clause of the document called for press freedom in both states.
Foreign reporters without accreditation may face legal problems in Belarus. They are also barred from attending official press conferences or interviewing government officials.
Sheremet told Reuters on Tuesday he saw the ministry move as a renewal of pressure on the mass media in the republic.

In March, Belarus ordered a reporter for Russia's NTV television network to leave the country, first cancelling his accreditation. Lukashenko then accused foreign media, including Russian, of bias in reporting opposition protests.
The Belarussian leader is widely seen in the West as increasingly authoritarian, especially after he used a controversial referendum last year to crack down on the opposition and increase his powers.
